newsitem.title: FRANCE: Renaissance masters inspire Saint Laurent couture.
newsitem.headline: Renaissance masters inspire Saint Laurent couture.

text.p: Yves Saint Laurent looked to the old masters to inspire his Autumn/Winter haute couture collection on Wednesday, a sombre parade of gowns echoing the royal courts of the Renaissance.

Black velvet princess gowns, their waists elongated, and rounded necklines edged with rich sable, recalled the shadowed works of Clouet, court painter to France's Valois dynasty, Flemish artist Frans Hals and the mistresses of French kings.
Gold crosses dangled from models' necks and feathers shivered atop Shakespearean caps.
The flowers of a mediaeval tapestry trickled down pinegreen velvet sleeves and period gems and gilt filigree glistened from the collar of a dark robe.
The embroidered, jewel-encrusted bolero made a comeback, as did Saint Laurent's signature black "smoking" evening suits, here with masculine tailoring and cumberbunds or simple and classically cut.
Tweed suits and flannel jumpsuits in muted hues of seaweed, lichen, beige and cocoa provided classic daywear that caught the eye when brightened by a pair of violet gloves or turqoise hats.
Fur, genuine fox, sable and mink, seemed to be everywear, for indoors and out -- on hats, shawls, the cuffs of gloves and as trim on gowns or suits.

"I was inspired by the black in Clouet's portraits, the gowns of Diane de Poitiers, the portraits of the de Medicis. I thought of the darkness of Rembrandt ciseled with gold and sable and of the very pure elongated shape of the body," Saint Laurent told reporters.
"Nothing is left but the line of the body. Unfortunately it makes me suffer more and more because it's very difficult."

At Balmain, U.S. designer Oscar de la Renta took his collection beyond the house's prim and proper limits, sending out a red and gold velvet brocade coat for a night at the opera and slinky georgette slip dresses strewn with pearls.
Chiffon boudoir robes embroidered with 16th century Italian motifs brought bursts of applause.
Paisley dustcoats edged with sable or jet-embroidered pale jackets over billowing dance skirts summoned up images of the Orient's influence on the Belle Epoque.
Satin ballgowns festooned with flowers and trimmed with luscious furs were gleaned from the wardrobes of turn-of-the century Russian nobility.
The daywear was classic and demure for Balmain's mature American clientele, with tweed suits, a chocolate suede maxi and one flashy trouser ensemble of cranberry floral satin.
Paco Rabanne went cosmic, showing tube dresses matched with jackets of plexi-glass cubes paraded to music from Star Wars.
There was a bustier gown of road pavement, a bell-shaped skirt of compressed household rubbish repainted bluish, and a plastic and ostrich feather raincoat that encased a model's head.
